https://www.baltictimes.com/latvia_s_exp.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Latvia’s experience in countering malicious hybrid attacks is invaluable - Estonian minister 2026-07-23 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - Latvia’s experience in countering malicious hybrid attacks is invaluable, said Estonian Minister of the Interior Igor Taro, who met with his Latvian counterpart Janis Dombrava (National Alliance) in Latvia this week. The Latvian Ministry of the Interior informed LETA that Dombrava hosted the Estonian Minister of the Interior during his working visit to Latvia. During the visit, the ministers discussed cooperation between the two countries in the areas of border security, migration management, civil protection and crisis management, as well as familiarized themselves with Latvia’s internal security infrastructure and the work of its internal affairs services. Dombrava noted that he and his Estonian counterpart are in agreement-the security challenges in the Baltics are becoming increasingly complex, which is why close cooperation between both countries is essential, and only by working together can we ensure a secure Baltic region and a strong external border of the European Union (EU). During the meeting, Taro emphasized that Latvia is not only Estonia’s closest neighbor, but also one of its most reliable allies. Latvia’s experience in countering malicious hybrid attacks is invaluable, and both the Estonian Police and the Estonian Border Guard are gaining valuable and irreplaceable experience by sending their officers to assist their Latvian colleagues in countering these deliberately created challenges. This cooperation will undoubtedly continue, Taro emphasized. On the first day of the visit, the Latvian and Estonian ministers of the interior visited the disaster management centers in Salacgriva and Saulkrasti, where they familiarized themselves with Latvia’s civil protection and crisis management system, local governments’ preparedness for emergencies and mechanisms for inter-agency cooperation. They discussed the role of disaster management centers in the civil protection system, coordinating cooperation between state and local government agencies and ensuring a rapid response to various types of threats. The ministers also visited the port of Skulte, where they discussed the port’s importance to the country’s security infrastructure. The visit continued in Mucenieki, where the ministers familiarized themselves with the work of the Asylum Seekers’ Center and the Detention Center for Foreign Nationals, discussing the management of migration flows, procedures for accommodating foreign nationals, and inter-institutional cooperation. Meanwhile, at the Riga Municipal Police Unified Command and Video Surveillance Center, the delegation learned about digital solutions for ensuring public safety and order, the use of video surveillance systems, and the coordination of rapid response operations. On the second day of the visit, Taro, together with Edvins Snore (National Alliance), Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of the Interior, visited the Latvian-Belarusian state border, the Silene Border Guard Unit, the Ludza Precinct of the State Police, the State Border Guard Special Operations Service Sigma, and the Terehova Border Control Point. During the visit, special attention was paid to the security of the EU external border, border surveillance infrastructure, the operational capabilities of the services, as well as the experience of the Baltic states and Poland in countering the migration pressure exerted by the Belarusian regime. Latvian officials thanked Estonia for the practical support provided to the Latvian State Border Guard during the period of enhanced border security operations. At the conclusion of the visit, the delegation met with representatives of the Aluksne Municipality to discuss current security issues facing border municipalities, civil protection and crisis management issues, as well as the challenges municipalities face in the current geopolitical situation. During the meeting, cooperation between the national government and local governments was also discussed, with a focus on strengthening resilience and preparedness for various potential crisis situations. https://www.politico.eu/article/europes-.text: The brutally hot summer is set to cost the EU economy €180 billion this year — that’s equivalent to roughly 1 percent of GDP, which is all the growth the bloc was expected to generate in 2026, according to new analysis. France could lose 1.4 percentage points of growth, which is enough to push its economy into a 0.6 percent contraction, while an 0.8-point hit could almost wipe out the Netherlands’ expected expansion. “The result is not simply ‘the hottest countries lose the most,'” notes the analysis by Triodos Bank . “Spain and Italy have the highest physical exposure and the most hot days in absolute terms, but decades of acclimatisation imply that the marginal effect of any single hot day is comparatively small.” Advertisement Advertisement The biggest drag is expected to come from people struggling to work in extreme heat. Triodos estimates lost labor productivity alone could shave around 0.6 percent off EU GDP, while agricultural output could fall by between 3 and 7 percent. “At first sight this might seem modest, but it is exactly the expected economic growth for the EU this year,” said the bank of the overall €180 billion blow. And the summer is not over. France and Britain are bracing for their fifth heat wave of the season this week, with temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius in southeastern France and 36 degrees forecast in the U.K. The bill is already mounting beyond GDP. POLITICO estimated at least 14,000 excess deaths across the six hardest-hit European countries during the record-breaking heat wave from mid-June to early July. Drought has also hammered Europe’s energy system: Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp cuts at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant and pushed Romania to blast apart a rock to divert water toward its last operating reactor. Vessels on the Rhine and Danube have had to sail only partially loaded. In Austria, meanwhile, drought has caused an estimated €1 billion in agricultural losses , according to Austrian Hail Insurance, after some regions received more than 75 percent less rain than normal since mid-June. Triodos warned against treating this summer as a freak event, saying extreme heat “might become structural” as the planet warms. But governments can soften the damage through irrigation, insulation, cooling and shifting working hours, said the bank. “Every year adaptation without mitigation is a year borrowed against a hotter baseline.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://arynews.tv/twelve-killed-and-at-.text: International Twelve killed and at least 10 injured in Polish bus crash in Hungary By Reuters - Aug 16, 2026 Add ARY News on Google A A Resize BUDAPEST: A dozen people were killed and at least 10 seriously injured after a Polish bus carrying 57 pilgrims veered off a ​motorway in eastern Hungary, in an accident that a survivor described as “unimaginable”. Hungarian Prime ‌Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday in a Facebook post that the bus had run into a ditch and tipped over at around 1 a.m. The bus, which also had two drivers on board, was returning to Poland ​from a shrine to the Virgin Mary at Medjugorje in southeastern Bosnia. The injured were ​taken to hospitals in four nearby cities. Crash survivor Helena Tluczek, from Lubenia, told ⁠Reuters from her hospital bed that she was on the phone with a friend back ​in Poland when the bus suddenly tipped over, and rolled. She suffered broken ribs and injuries to ​her shoulder and spine, and also hit her head, but remembered some of what had happened. “All the seats were ripped out. People were under the seats; everyone was screaming for help,” she said. She pulled two people ​out from under the wreckage and then “clawed my way out of that vehicle with my ​hands”. Tluczek managed to pull her sister out of the bus before collapsing. “When I looked back, it was like … Mother ‌of ⁠Jesus… It is not possible; it is unimaginable to see what it looked like inside that bus,” she added. The accident happened near the town of Mezokeresztes in eastern Hungary, police said, on the way towards the city of Nyiregyhaza. Pictures from the scene showed a badly damaged red bus ​lying on its side in ​a ditch by ⁠the motorway with windows smashed and belongings and suitcases scattered around. “A Polish-registered bus … veered off the straight stretch of road into a ditch and ​overturned. Preliminary information suggests the driver likely fell asleep,” police said on ​their website, ⁠adding that the driver was being taken into custody. Polish President Karol Nawrocki said on X: “It is with deep sorrow that I received the tragic news of the Polish bus accident in Hungary, in which ⁠so many ​of our compatriots died.” In July 2002, a tourist bus ​carrying Polish pilgrims flipped over at a roundabout near Lake Balaton in western Hungary, killing 20 people. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/iran.text: Iran's parliament voted 174 to six on Tuesday to pass an article banning Iranian nationals from giving interviews to or participating in discussions with media outlets designated as "hostile" by the Intelligence Ministry, or with outlets owned, managed or funded by operatives connected to countries classified as adversaries of the Islamic Republic.Violations of Article 22 of the bill on "countering the penetration of intelligence services and foreign governments or entities" carry sixth-degree penalties under the Islamic Penal Code, including imprisonment of more than six months up to two years, fines, 31 to 74 lashes, deprivation of social rights and other restrictions.The bill classifies foreign governments into two tiers: a "level 1 government" is a state formally designated as hostile under Iranian law or by decision of the Supreme National Security Council."Level 2" is defined as a state that has planned or carried out actions aimed at damaging Tehran's political, defence, security, economic, social or cultural interests.The list of level two governments is to be drawn up by the Intelligence Ministry and the IRGC intelligence organisation, then approved by the Supreme National Security Council.A proposal by Tehran MP Alireza Salimi to exempt government officials from the scope of Article 22 was also approved at the same sitting.President Masoud Pezeshkian's cabinet had formally opposed the bill. At its 22 August meeting, the cabinet said the legislation had "serious flaws," including restrictions on scientific activity, the acceleration of elite emigration and negative consequences at national and international level.First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref had warned of consequences for science and technology. Presidential legal deputy Majid Ansari said "criminalising broad and general categories in this bill could harm citizens' rights."Parliament also passed Article 20 of the same bill, under which anyone who accesses unpublished official information by virtue of their job may not share it with a foreign agent without prior authorisation. The penalty is four to 10 years in prison and a permanent bar from the post through which the information was accessed.The legislation follows months of hardline rhetoric from Iranian officials against Persian-language broadcasters outside Iran.On 26 August, armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi accused BBC Persian, Iran International and Radio Farda of links to US and Israeli intelligence organisations and said their staff could be placed in the Islamic Republic's "military targets bank".Following the parliamentary vote, the bill still needs further approval to become law. The Majlis must complete its examination of remaining articles before sending the text to the Guardian Council, which reviews legislation for compatibility with Sharia and the constitution.If the Guardian Council raises objections and the Majlis insists on its position, the Expediency Council makes a final ruling.The parliament that passed the article emerged from elections in which turnout was reportedly at around 41%, the lowest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.Turnout in Tehran was around 24%. The leading candidate in the capital won some 598,000 votes, compared with more than 1.6 million for the leading Tehran candidate in the 2016 elections.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6ly.text: Image source, Reuters/Handout Image caption, The people of Oleshky have had no electricity for years and no access to food or water By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor ,Â Olga Malchevska Â and Â Dan Johnson ,Â in Kyiv Published 1 hour ago A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources. Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous. However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported. US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys. That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region. Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave. An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas. Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave. Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process". A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022". Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself. Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack. One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation. Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire. Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire. On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys". Image source, Ksenia Arkhipova Image caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday. Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices". Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon. Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions. Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground. Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets Image caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians. Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger. Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys". White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster' Published 3 days ago Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water Published 24 September To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city Published 6 May Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there". He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine. One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation". However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible. Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports. "Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne. Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv. https://www.dw.com/en/brazil-s-new-anti-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OpTu Prefer DW on Google Residents of the "Complexa da Penha" favela in Rio watch in shock as bodies laid out in the street are being removed. More than 130 people were killed during the police operation on October 28, 2025 Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP/Getty Images Advertisement One year after the deadliest police operation in the history of Brazil , human rights organization Human Rights Watch (HRW) has leveled serious accusations against the country's authorities. Contrary to legal regulations, most of the 2,500 police officers who were deployed to the "Complexo do Alemao" and "Complexo da Penha" favelas on October 28, 2025, did not wear body cameras. In the course of "Operacao Contencao" ("Operation Containment"), police officers were expected to execute dozens of arrest warrants against members of the Comando Vermelho drug cartel that day. The result: During hours-long firefights in the favelas, 117 alleged gang members and five police officers were killed. Brazil election: Voters in Rio split over crime and policing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Body cameras don't show the full picture After analyzing more than 4,000 hours of video material, HRW concluded in its investigation that only around one quarter of the deployed police officers were wearing body cameras and that some were manipulated. Not a single deadly shooting was captured on camera. "It's clear to us that a decision by the Supreme Court according to which the police in Rio must wear body cameras was violated," said HRW Brazil director Cesar Munoz. The organization published its report in Rio de Janeiro on October 28. Having analyzed the autopsy findings, HRW also concludes that many bodies show signs of execution, i.e. the killing of persons already incapable of fighting. Excessive police violence: According to HRW, 40% of those killed were shot in the head and 75% were shot in the back Image: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance For example, 40% of those killed were shot in the head, and 75% were shot in the back. There were reasons to believe, Munoz said, that the operation "was obviously designed to be lethal." The police operation carried out under the supervision of the state government of Rio de Janeiro shocked the country. However, there were soon calls to intensify the fight against organized crime. Fighting drug gangs and militias In response, the "Anti-gang Law" ("Lei Antifaccao") came into force in March 2026. It is aimed at combating criminal gangs like the PCC, a drug gang based in Sao Paulo, or the Comando Vermelho (CV), which dominates Rio. However, militias (gangs made up of corrupt police officers and soldiers) are also to be dismantled, both criminally and economically. "The law addresses a real problem," Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety (FBSP) NGO told DW. This was because the ability of criminal organizations to control territories, move funds and make inroads into economic activities and public institutions had expanded. Police and military operations in Rio's favelas occur time and again. The "Anti-Gang Law" of March 2026 expands the police's powers in the fight against drug gangs Image: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance It was positive, he added, that the law extends tools for asset tracing, finance tracking, institutional cooperation and capital withdrawal to these organizations. Another improvement, said HRW Brazil's Cesar Munoz, was closer cooperation between state security agencies. The federal police, which reports to the central government, was to play a greater role in combating gangs in the future. In Brazil, military and civil police report to state governments. During the deadly operations in Rio de Janeiro's favelas, one year ago, command was under the authority of the state government of Rio de Janeiro — and, consequently, under the influence of local politics. Overcrowded prisons and recruitment behind bars On the other hand, however, the law was raising constitutional concerns, said the FBSP's Azevedo. For example, it provides for the automatic imposition of pretrial detention on suspects. Residents of a favela in Rio protest against police violence during operations targeting drug dealers in their neighborhood Image: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance Other plans included expansion of grounds for arrest, restrictions on the easing of prison conditions — such as furloughs and the suspension of the remainder of a sentence — as well as an extension of the length of stay in prisons. This could further exacerbate Brazil's chronic prison overcrowding. "Brazil already has one of the largest prison populations worldwide, and the law could accelerate its growth," said Azevedo. In addition, prison overcrowding in Brazil had the perverse side effect of allowing crime syndicates such as the PCC and Comando Vermelho to recruit new members there. "Overcrowded prisons without adequate government control facilitate recruitment and strengthening of the very criminal factions that legislation intend to combat," Azevedo concluded. "It would be important to prevent gangs from recruiting young people and to show those who've committed crimes new prospects in life," HRW's Cesar Munoz told DW. Brazil has one of the largest prison populations in the world Image: Jonne Roriz/dpa/picture-alliance Rodrigo Ghiringhelli de Azevedo of FBSP also sees a constitutional problem in the cancellation of prison assistance — a benefit that the state paid to the prisoners' dependents. "Its cancellation means economic punishment for those who haven't committed any crime at all, including children. This runs afoul of the constitutional principle according to which punishments must not extend beyond the convicted person," Azevedo said. This article was originally published in German.
